title: Penrose tiling
hook: Two tile shapes that cover a floor forever without the pattern ever repeating.
peek: In 1974 Roger Penrose found a pair of tiles that fill a floor completely but never settle into a repeating pattern. Years later, a chemist found crystals whose atoms are ordered in the same strange, never-repeating way.
lede: Ordinary floor tiles repeat: shift the pattern and it lines up with itself. In 1974 the mathematician Roger Penrose found two shapes, now called the kite and the dart, that can tile a floor endlessly but only in patterns that never repeat. The tilings are full of fivefold, starlike symmetry, which no repeating tiling can have.

bullets.text: Both shapes come from one rhombus cut in two, and all their angles are multiples of 36 degrees. Markings on the edges stop them fitting into a repeating layout. Over a large patch, kites outnumber darts by the golden ratio, about 1.618 to 1.

In 1982 the chemist Dan Shechtman saw fivefold symmetry in a rapidly cooled alloy of aluminium and manganese, a pattern textbooks said crystals could not have. Many colleagues dismissed it. The atoms proved to be ordered much like a Penrose tiling, and he won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

In 2007 the physicists Peter Lu and Paul Steinhardt argued that a 15th-century shrine in Isfahan, Iran, carries tilework very close to a Penrose pattern. Its makers seem to have used a small set of standard tile shapes, centuries before the mathematics was written down.
